VIDEO.title: Matthew 12:22-37 – What Is The Sin That Can Never Be Forgiven?
VIDEO.series: The Gospel of Matthew Every Word (playlist of 58 videos)

hand: The tree is known by its fruit.
SUMMARY: The teacher reads Matthew 12:22-37. Jesus heals a demon-possessed man who is blind and mute, and the crowds ask, 'Can this man really be the Son of David?' The Pharisees answer that He casts out demons by Beelzebul. Jesus replies with a divided kingdom and a bound strong man, warns that blasphemy against the Spirit will not be forgiven, and says a tree is known by its fruit and people will give account for every careless word.

Beelzebul is understood by many scholars as a Greek form of 'Baal Zebul,' 'Prince Baal.' By Jesus' time the title was given to Satan. The Pharisees could not deny the exorcisms, so they said He worked by Satan's power.

Why would an exorcism make people think of the Son of David? There was an expectation that the Messiah would cast out demons. Psalms found among the Dead Sea Scrolls present David as one who sang over the possessed, which sheds light on David playing the harp for Saul when an evil spirit troubled him (1 Samuel 16).

Jesus Himself defines blasphemy against the Spirit in context: attributing the Spirit's work to Satan. The Old Testament frame is sinning 'with a high hand' (Numbers 15:30-31), calling evil good (Isaiah 5:20, 24), and the warning of Hebrews 6:4-6.

Tree and fruit: Jews called a person's mitzvot (deeds) the fruit on the tree of halakha. A person's actions prove their theology. 'Careless' words (argos) are literally workless, deedless words, so Jesus is again talking about fruit, as in Matthew 7:15-20.

The lesson repeats last week's: lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God. The Pharisees had a bad eye (ayin ra'ah), and it filled them with darkness.
QUOTES: The actions of a person proves their theology.
Jesus defines what blasphemy against the spirit is.
You cannot produce good fruit if the heart is filled with poison.
Lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God.

method.p: The teacher's tip on a famously hard saying: do not read one verse alone. Ask what Jesus is responding to, and let the context define the term. Here, the Pharisees' claim in 12:24 tells you what blasphemy against the Spirit is.

STRONGMAN.title: Can this be the Son of David?

src.text: Then a demon-possessed man who was blind and mute was brought to Jesus, and He healed him, so that the mute man spoke and saw. And all the crowds were astounded, and were saying, “Can this man really be the Son of David?” But when the Pharisees heard this, they said, “This man does not cast out demons except by Beelzebul the ruler of the demons.”

lines.text: The crowds' reaction, wondering if He is the Messiah, seems to be what pushed the Pharisees to say something so horrific.

Beelzebul is understood by many scholars as a Greek form of 'Baal Zebul,' 'Prince Baal.' The video cites Michael Heiser: Baal was ruler of the gods, of the earth and of the underworld, where demons were believed to dwell. By Jesus' time the title was given to Satan.
The Pharisees had made the same charge before (9:34; 10:25).

src.text: Thus it happened that whenever the evil spirit from God came to Saul, David would take the harp and play it with his hand; and Saul would be refreshed and be well, and the evil spirit would depart from him.

lines.text: Why would an exorcism make people say 'Son of David'? There was an expectation that the Messiah would cast out demons. It is unclear where in the Old Testament that came from.

Psalms found among the Dead Sea Scrolls suggest David was remembered as an exorcist who sang over the possessed. That sheds light on 1 Samuel 16, and may explain why the Son of David was expected to do what David did.
The Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 credits David with thousands of psalms and songs, including four songs to be sung over the afflicted.

src.text: But if I cast out demons by the Spirit of God, then the kingdom of God has come upon you. Or how can anyone enter the strong man’s house and carry off his property, unless he first binds the strong man? And then he will plunder his house.

lines.text: Jesus answers their thoughts: a kingdom divided against itself cannot stand. If He drives out demons by the Spirit of God, the kingdom of God has come.
Luke's version: 'by the finger of God' (Luke 11:20), which recalls Pharaoh's magicians in Exodus 8:19.

src.text: “Therefore I say to you, any sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, either in this age or in the age to come.

lines.text: Jesus defines the sin in context. It answers the claim that He cast out demons by the ruler of demons: blasphemy against the Spirit is attributing the work of the Spirit to Satan.
It is not ignorance. The Pharisees knew He had done miracles and knew what that could mean; refusing Him as Messiah, they reached for an explanation that would undermine Him.
Mark explains: 'because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit”' (Mark 3:30).

src.text: But the person who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native or a sojourner, that one is blaspheming Yahweh; and that person shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised the word of Yahweh and has broken His commandment, that person shall be completely cut off; his guilt will be on him.’”

lines.text: There is no single Old Testament text behind Jesus' words, but a few can be pieced together. His hearers would likely have thought of sinning with a high hand: defiant, persistent rejection of God and His commands.
Notice the finality: cut off, and then completely cut off.

left.text: Therefore, as a tongue of fire consumes stubble / And dry grass collapses into the flame, / So their root will become like rot and their blossom blow away as dust; / For they have rejected the law of Yahweh of hosts / And the word of the Holy One of Israel they have spurned.

right.text: and having fallen away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance, since they again crucify to themselves the Son of God and put Him to open shame.

lines.text: Isaiah 5:20 sounds like the Pharisees: calling evil good and good evil. Their root will rot because they despised God's word. The same thread runs through all three passages: those who despise and reject God cannot be forgiven.

Anyone who looks at God's activity and says 'That's the devil' will never submit to the Lord. How the unforgiveness works is unclear; many suggest it is a persistent rejection of the only means of salvation.

FRUIT.title: The tree is known by its fruit

src.text: “Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruit. You brood of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak what is good? For the mouth speaks out of that which fills the heart. The good man brings out of his good treasure what is good; and the evil man brings out of his evil treasure what is evil.

lines.text: Halakha is how one walks out the Torah; mitzvot are the deeds. Jews called a person's mitzvot the fruit on the tree of halakha. So a person's actions prove their theology.
If a teacher's theology does not make him and his students lowly, merciful, loving, radically generous children of God, it doesn't matter what he teaches: the fruit is rotten.
John the Baptist called the Pharisees and Sadducees a 'brood of vipers' first (3:7); Jesus does again in 23:33.

src.text: You will know them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thorn bushes or figs from thistles? Even so, every good tree bears good fruit, but the bad tree bears bad fruit. A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit.

lines.text: Jesus taught about trees and fruit in the Sermon on the Mount. Matthew 12 is Jesus walking out what He taught in Matthew 7. And the Pharisees' fruit? Calling the Spirit of God the power of the devil.
Their reaction shows what they treasure (6:21): knowing and following the rules more than knowing the One who made them.

src.text: But I tell you that every careless word that people speak, they shall give an accounting for it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”

lines.text: 'Careless' is not an accidental slip. The word means workless or deedless: again Jesus is talking about mitzvot, which show a person's halakha and their heart.
The Pharisees did not have God's good eye; they had an ayin ra'ah, a bad eye, and it filled the whole body with darkness (6:22-23).

TERMS.def: 'Baal Zebul,' 'Prince Baal'; a name for the ruler of demons. The captions spell it 'Beelible.'
A title for the Messiah, the promised king from David's line.
In context, attributing the work of God's Spirit to Satan (12:24, 31-32).
Sinning 'with a high hand': open, defiant rejection of God's word (Numbers 15:30).
From 'to walk': how one walks out the Torah in life.
Commandments, and the deeds that keep them; the fruit on the tree of halakha.
Hebrew 'bad eye': stinginess and lack of mercy (6:23). The captions write 'ain raha.'
'Offspring of snakes': a sharp name for leaders whose words poison (3:7; 12:34; 23:33).

WORDS.gloss: Beelzebul, ruler of the demons. Look up: BDAG, Βεελζεβούλ.
Idle, useless; literally 'not working.' Look up: BDAG, ἀργός.
To be high, lifted up; 'with a high hand.'
To revile, blaspheme. Look up: BDB or HALOT, גָּדַף.

BACKGROUND.p: Jesus asks, 'by whom do your sons cast them out?' (12:27). Jewish exorcists were known in the first century; Josephus tells of one named Eleazar who used incantations attributed to Solomon (Antiquities 8.2.5).

The Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11Q5) ends with a prose note crediting David with 3,600 psalms and many songs, including four songs to be sung over the afflicted. Another Cave 11 scroll (11Q11) preserves psalms against demons linked to David and Solomon.
In Canaanite texts from Ugarit, Baal is called zbl, 'prince.' Baal-zebub ('lord of flies') in 2 Kings 1:2 may be a mocking change of Baal-zebul ('Baal the prince').
The Law offered sacrifices for unintentional sins (Numbers 15:22-29) but none for defiant ones (15:30-31). Later Jewish teaching kept this distinction between error and rebellion.

DEBATES.p: The video ties the sin to the Pharisees' deliberate rejection of what they knew was God's work. Many pastors add that those who fear they have committed it show by that fear that they have not; others focus on persistent, final unbelief.

DEBATES.h: Did the Messiah have to be an exorcist?
DEBATES.p: The video admits it is unclear where the expectation came from and points to David and the Qumran psalms. Others note that Jewish texts more often link exorcism with Solomon, the son of David.

The video reads them along one thread: rejecting God after seeing His work. Interpreters differ on whether Hebrews 6 describes true believers, a hypothetical warning, or people who tasted without believing.

CAREFUL_INTRO: Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
CAREFUL: The video says 12:23 is the only place where Jesus has such an effect on the crowds. After a similar healing of a mute demoniac, 'the crowds marveled' (9:33), and others call Him 'Son of David' in 9:27, 15:22, 20:30 and 21:9.
The second Beelzebul passage is Matthew 10:25 (the captions say '10:2').
'Only in the Gospel of Matthew' do words reflect character: Luke has the same saying, 'his mouth speaks from the abundance of his heart' (Luke 6:45).
Matthew 7:15-20 warns against false prophets; the video applies it to the Pharisees and Israel's leaders, which is a reading, not what the text says outright.
The claims credited to Michael Heiser about Baal and the underworld are summaries we could not check against his books.
The captions spell Beelzebul 'Beelible,' the Gadarenes 'Gatherines,' and the Hebrew ayin ra'ah 'ain raha.'

QUESTIONS: Why do you think the Pharisees chose 'Beelzebul' over 'maybe He is the Messiah'?
How does reading 12:24 change the way you understand the unforgivable sin?
What fruit does your theology produce in your week: mercy, generosity, humility?
Which of your words this week would you call 'workless'? Which were full of good treasure?
Where might you be valuing the rules more than the One who made them?
Read Isaiah 29:13. How can you guard against honoring God with your lips while your heart is far away?
APPLICATION_VIDEO: The same lesson runs from the start of chapter 12: lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God. Jesus' condemnation of the Pharisees is a warning to everyone: either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make it bad. Don't be a hypocrite, doing things for God while your heart is filled with hatred; you cannot produce good fruit if the heart is filled with poison. It is not enough to say good, true things about God; what matters is aligning our hearts with God's heart, as in the Beatitudes. If God's people do that, they will be generous and merciful like their Father, and they will not miss the activity of God in their midst. We ask what God is doing around us, but do we consider the condition of our own heart? The Lord said His people honored Him with their lips while their hearts were far from Him (Isaiah 29:13), and Jesus will quote it to the Pharisees in Matthew 15. Is hypocrisy, rooted in a lack of mercy, your problem or mine?
APPLICATION_ADDED: Study note (added): this week, write down three things you said that you would not want to give account for, and three that came from good treasure. Ask the Spirit to make the tree good, and look for one place to show mercy where you have been quick to judge.

## The sin that will not be forgiven
1. Matthew 12:31-32: Blasphemy against the Spirit
   Defined Matthew 12:31-32: "“Therefore I say to you, any sin and blasphemy shall be forgiven people, but the blasphemy against the Spirit shall not be forgiven. And whoever speaks a word against the Son of Man, it shall be forgiven him; but whoever speaks against the Holy Spirit, it shall not be forgiven him, either in this age or in the age to come." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+12:31-32
   (video) Jesus defines the sin in context. It answers the claim that He cast out demons by the ruler of demons: blasphemy against the Spirit is attributing the work of the Spirit to Satan.
   (video) It is not ignorance. The Pharisees knew He had done miracles and knew what that could mean; refusing Him as Messiah, they reached for an explanation that would undermine Him.
   [Background] Mark explains: 'because they were saying, “He has an unclean spirit”' (Mark 3:30). (Mark 3:28-30)
2. Numbers 15:30-31: With a high hand
   Defiance Numbers 15:30-31: "But the person who does anything with a high hand, whether he is native or a sojourner, that one is blaspheming Yahweh; and that person shall be cut off from among his people. Because he has despised the word of Yahweh and has broken His commandment, that person shall be completely cut off; his guilt will be on him.’”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Numbers+15:30-31
   (video) There is no single Old Testament text behind Jesus' words, but a few can be pieced together. His hearers would likely have thought of sinning with a high hand: defiant, persistent rejection of God and His commands.
   (video) Notice the finality: cut off, and then completely cut off.
3. Isaiah 5 and Hebrews 6: Calling evil good
   Isaiah (Isaiah 5:24, LSB): "Therefore, as a tongue of fire consumes stubble / And dry grass collapses into the flame, / So their root will become like rot and their blossom blow away as dust; / For they have rejected the law of Yahweh of hosts / And the word of the Holy One of Israel they have spurned."
   Hebrews (Hebrews 6:6, LSB): "and having fallen away, it is impossible to renew them again to repentance, since they again crucify to themselves the Son of God and put Him to open shame."
   (video) Isaiah 5:20 sounds like the Pharisees: calling evil good and good evil. Their root will rot because they despised God's word. The same thread runs through all three passages: those who despise and reject God cannot be forgiven. (Isaiah 5:20)
   (video) Anyone who looks at God's activity and says 'That's the devil' will never submit to the Lord. How the unforgiveness works is unclear; many suggest it is a persistent rejection of the only means of salvation.

## The tree and its fruit
1. Matthew 12:33-35: The tree is known by its fruit
   Mitzvot Matthew 12:33-35: "“Either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make the tree bad and its fruit bad; for the tree is known by its fruit. You brood of vipers, how can you, being evil, speak what is good? For the mouth speaks out of that which fills the heart. The good man brings out of his good treasure what is good; and the evil man brings out of his evil treasure what is evil." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+12:33-35
   (video) Halakha is how one walks out the Torah; mitzvot are the deeds. Jews called a person's mitzvot the fruit on the tree of halakha. So a person's actions prove their theology.
   (video) If a teacher's theology does not make him and his students lowly, merciful, loving, radically generous children of God, it doesn't matter what he teaches: the fruit is rotten.
   [Background] John the Baptist called the Pharisees and Sadducees a 'brood of vipers' first (3:7); Jesus does again in 23:33. (Matthew 3:7; Matthew 23:33)
2. Matthew 7:15-20: Grapes from thorn bushes?
   Echo Matthew 7:16-18: "You will know them by their fruits. Are grapes gathered from thorn bushes or figs from thistles? Even so, every good tree bears good fruit, but the bad tree bears bad fruit. A good tree cannot bear bad fruit, nor can a bad tree bear good fruit." https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+7:16-18
   (video) Jesus taught about trees and fruit in the Sermon on the Mount. Matthew 12 is Jesus walking out what He taught in Matthew 7. And the Pharisees' fruit? Calling the Spirit of God the power of the devil.
   (video) Their reaction shows what they treasure (6:21): knowing and following the rules more than knowing the One who made them. (Matthew 6:21)
3. Matthew 12:36-37: Every careless word
   Argos Matthew 12:36-37: "But I tell you that every careless word that people speak, they shall give an accounting for it in the day of judgment. For by your words you will be justified, and by your words you will be condemned.”" https://read.lsbible.org/?q=Matthew+12:36-37
   (video) 'Careless' is not an accidental slip. The word means workless or deedless: again Jesus is talking about mitzvot, which show a person's halakha and their heart.
   (video) The Pharisees did not have God's good eye; they had an ayin ra'ah, a bad eye, and it filled the whole body with darkness (6:22-23). (Matthew 6:22-23)

## Key people
- Jesus: Heals the blind and mute man by the Spirit of God and defines blasphemy against the Spirit. [Background] Matthew has already shown the Spirit coming on Him at His baptism (3:16) and quoted Isaiah: 'I will put My Spirit upon Him' (12:18).
- The blind and mute man: Demon-possessed; healed so that he spoke and saw. [Background] Luke records the same healing (Luke 11:14).
- The crowds: Astounded, they ask if He is the Son of David. [Background] Others call Jesus 'Son of David' in Matthew 9:27; 15:22; 20:30; 21:9.
- The Pharisees: Say He casts out demons by Beelzebul: a bad eye and rotten fruit. [Background] Mark names 'the scribes who came down from Jerusalem' (Mark 3:22).
- Beelzebul: 'Prince Baal,' by Jesus' time a title for Satan. [Background] Compare Baal-zebub, 'the god of Ekron' (2 Kings 1:2).
- David and Saul: David's harp drove the evil spirit from Saul. [Background] Saul later tried to kill David while he played (1 Samuel 18:10-11).

## Places [Background]
- Capernaum: Jesus' base in Galilee; Matthew does not name the town of this healing.
- Gadara (named in the video): The video recalls the possessed men among the tombs of the Gadarenes (8:28); the captions say 'Gatherines.'
- Ekron: Philistine city whose god was Baal-zebub (2 Kings 1:2).
- Gibeah: Saul's home and royal seat (1 Samuel 15:34), where David came to play for him.
- Qumran (named in the video): Where the Dead Sea Scrolls were found, including the Psalms Scroll that credits David with songs over the afflicted.

## Key terms
- Beelzebul: 'Baal Zebul,' 'Prince Baal'; a name for the ruler of demons. The captions spell it 'Beelible.'
- Son of David: A title for the Messiah, the promised king from David's line.
- Blasphemy against the Spirit: In context, attributing the work of God's Spirit to Satan (12:24, 31-32).
- High hand: Sinning 'with a high hand': open, defiant rejection of God's word (Numbers 15:30).
- Halakha: From 'to walk': how one walks out the Torah in life.
- Mitzvot: Commandments, and the deeds that keep them; the fruit on the tree of halakha.
- Ayin ra'ah: Hebrew 'bad eye': stinginess and lack of mercy (6:23). The captions write 'ain raha.'
- Brood of vipers: 'Offspring of snakes': a sharp name for leaders whose words poison (3:7; 12:34; 23:33).

## Historical and cultural background [Background: established]
- Exorcists in Jesus' day: Jesus asks, 'by whom do your sons cast them out?' (12:27). Jewish exorcists were known in the first century; Josephus tells of one named Eleazar who used incantations attributed to Solomon (Antiquities 8.2.5).
- David's songs at Qumran: The Psalms Scroll from Qumran Cave 11 (11Q5) ends with a prose note crediting David with 3,600 psalms and many songs, including four songs to be sung over the afflicted. Another Cave 11 scroll (11Q11) preserves psalms against demons linked to David and Solomon.
- Baal, prince and lord: In Canaanite texts from Ugarit, Baal is called zbl, 'prince.' Baal-zebub ('lord of flies') in 2 Kings 1:2 may be a mocking change of Baal-zebul ('Baal the prince').
- Sins with a high hand: The Law offered sacrifices for unintentional sins (Numbers 15:22-29) but none for defiant ones (15:30-31). Later Jewish teaching kept this distinction between error and rebellion.

## Where scholars differ [Background: debated]
- Can a believer commit it? The video ties the sin to the Pharisees' deliberate rejection of what they knew was God's work. Many pastors add that those who fear they have committed it show by that fear that they have not; others focus on persistent, final unbelief.
- Did the Messiah have to be an exorcist? The video admits it is unclear where the expectation came from and points to David and the Qumran psalms. Others note that Jewish texts more often link exorcism with Solomon, the son of David.
- Hebrews 6 and the unforgivable sin The video reads them along one thread: rejecting God after seeing His work. Interpreters differ on whether Hebrews 6 describes true believers, a hypothetical warning, or people who tasted without believing.

## Careful reading notes
Small slips worth knowing (offered gently; the video's main points stand):
- The video says 12:23 is the only place where Jesus has such an effect on the crowds. After a similar healing of a mute demoniac, 'the crowds marveled' (9:33), and others call Him 'Son of David' in 9:27, 15:22, 20:30 and 21:9.
- The second Beelzebul passage is Matthew 10:25 (the captions say '10:2').
- 'Only in the Gospel of Matthew' do words reflect character: Luke has the same saying, 'his mouth speaks from the abundance of his heart' (Luke 6:45).
- Matthew 7:15-20 warns against false prophets; the video applies it to the Pharisees and Israel's leaders, which is a reading, not what the text says outright.
- The claims credited to Michael Heiser about Baal and the underworld are summaries we could not check against his books.
- The captions spell Beelzebul 'Beelible,' the Gadarenes 'Gatherines,' and the Hebrew ayin ra'ah 'ain raha.'

## Reflection and discussion questions
1. Why do you think the Pharisees chose 'Beelzebul' over 'maybe He is the Messiah'?
2. How does reading 12:24 change the way you understand the unforgivable sin?
3. What fruit does your theology produce in your week: mercy, generosity, humility?
4. Which of your words this week would you call 'workless'? Which were full of good treasure?
5. Where might you be valuing the rules more than the One who made them?
6. Read Isaiah 29:13. How can you guard against honoring God with your lips while your heart is far away?

## Application
- (video) The same lesson runs from the start of chapter 12: lacking mercy leads to condemning what is not understood and becoming blind to the activity of God. Jesus' condemnation of the Pharisees is a warning to everyone: either make the tree good and its fruit good, or make it bad. Don't be a hypocrite, doing things for God while your heart is filled with hatred; you cannot produce good fruit if the heart is filled with poison. It is not enough to say good, true things about God; what matters is aligning our hearts with God's heart, as in the Beatitudes. If God's people do that, they will be generous and merciful like their Father, and they will not miss the activity of God in their midst. We ask what God is doing around us, but do we consider the condition of our own heart? The Lord said His people honored Him with their lips while their hearts were far from Him (Isaiah 29:13), and Jesus will quote it to the Pharisees in Matthew 15. Is hypocrisy, rooted in a lack of mercy, your problem or mine?
- Study note (added): this week, write down three things you said that you would not want to give account for, and three that came from good treasure. Ask the Spirit to make the tree good, and look for one place to show mercy where you have been quick to judge.
